The final step checks out. Assuming the intermediate bound $d \ge n-m+2$, the Singleton inequality gives $km \le n(2m-1-n)$. Writing $n = 2m-j$ yields $km \le (2m-j)(j-1) = 2m(j-1) - j(j-1)$. If $j-1 < k/2$, then $k \ge 2j-1$, so $km \ge (2j-1)m > 2m(j-1) - j(j-1)$ (since $m > -j(j-1)$ always holds), a contradiction. Hence $j \ge \lceil k/2\rceil + 1 = \lfloor (k+3)/2\rfloor$, giving $n \le 2m - \lfloor (k+3)/2\rfloor$.

The solution glosses over the step "forces $k \le 2(j-1)$", but the cleaner inequality above avoids that gap.
